You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Vinh's Story

Vinh Tran, fifty-one, sits in the waiting room of the psychology clinic with his shoulders drawn inward, his back pressed firmly against the corner where two walls meet. He has positioned himself this way without conscious thought—it is simply where he feels least exposed. His wife, Linh, sits beside him, her hand resting on his knee. She came with him today because Vinh asked her to, though he has not fully explained why he finally made the appointment. The truth is he no longer knows how to live the way he has been living, and the exhaustion of maintaining it has become unbearable.

Three years ago, Vinh's marriage to David began to unravel in ways he could not have anticipated. They had been together for eighteen years, had built a life that appeared stable from the outside—a house in the suburbs, friends, family who had eventually come to accept them. But in the final months, David had become someone Vinh no longer recognized. The violence started small: a shove during an argument about money, a fist driven into Vinh's ribs one night when David came home drunk and convinced that Vinh had been unfaithful. The worst came on a Thursday evening when Vinh, tired from a long day of auditing financial records, made a casual comment about David's spending. David had pinned him against the kitchen counter, his forearm across Vinh's throat, and struck him repeatedly in the abdomen and face. Vinh remembered the shock of it more than the pain—the recognition that the person he had trusted completely was capable of this. He remembered fragments: David's face contorted with rage, the sound of his own voice asking why, the taste of blood. But there were gaps too, stretches of time that simply did not exist in his memory, as if his mind had shut down to protect itself.

Since then, Vinh has become a man defined by vigilance. At work, in his small office at the tax authority, he has rearranged his desk so that his chair faces the door and the wall behind him is solid. He tells colleagues it is for better lighting, but the truth is that he cannot concentrate if someone might approach from behind. When he is tired—and he is always tired now, his sleep fractured and poor—the hyperalertness becomes almost unbearable. His body interprets every sound in the office as a threat. Last month, when a colleague knocked on his door, Vinh's heart had raced so violently that he thought he was having a heart attack. Nothing was wrong. Nothing had ever been wrong. But his body does not believe this.

The unpredictability of daily life has become intolerable. When Linh suggests they go to a restaurant, Vinh finds himself calculating exits and sightlines before he agrees. If the lighting is wrong, if he cannot see who is entering, if he cannot position himself with a clear view of the room, he becomes anxious and withdrawn. Linh has stopped inviting him to social events. His sister no longer calls to ask him to family dinners. He has come to believe, with a certainty that feels absolute, that nothing good can happen to him anymore—that whatever he builds will be destroyed, that trust is a delusion, that he is fundamentally unsafe in the world.

What troubles him most is the sense that he has become something other than human. When he looks in the mirror, he sees a man who has been reduced to pure function: checking, monitoring, surviving. He feels like an object—a thing that responds to threat rather than a person who chooses how to live. The betrayal sits beneath everything, a wound that has not closed. He trusted David with his life, and David had used that trust as a weapon.

The fragments of memory arrive without warning. A flash of David's face. The pressure on his throat. And then it vanishes, leaving Vinh disoriented and shaking. At other times, the entire memory forces itself into his mind unbidden, usually late at night when he is already exhausted, and he lies awake replaying it until dawn.

Vinh finally came to this clinic because Linh told him she could not watch him disappear anymore. He is here because he is terrified of what he has become, and because some small part of him still hopes that there might be a way back to being a person rather than a prisoner of his own fear.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me: The vignette describes Vinh's hypervigilance extensively, including his need to position himself with his back to a wall and to see the room, his office rearrangement to face the door, and his general threat-monitoring behavior. However, there is no specific illustration or reference to the behavior of frequently looking behind him to check if someone is following him. While the vignette conveys a general sense of checking and monitoring, this particular threat-response behavior is not explicitly present.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
